chunks: Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-'Abbas ibn Ma'ruf and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Salt, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Abi al-Daylam, who said:
I said to Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام: A man drinks wine, then he spat, and some of his saliva fell upon my garment. He said: “It is nothing.”

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no ambiguity in this report, because he only asked him about the saliva of a wine-drinker, and he said there is no problem with it. Saliva is not najis; rather, what is najis is the wine. The Shaykh, may Allah Exalted support him, said: And the ruling of al-fuqqa' is likewise. This indicates that.

key_terms.النَّجَسُ: the najis thing; the substance judged ritually impure
key_terms.الْخَمْرَ: wine; the substance identified here as najis
key_terms.الْفُقَّاعِ: al-fuqqa'; an intoxicating beverage mentioned as sharing the same ruling
key_terms.بُصَاقِهِ: his saliva/spittle; the substance asked about in the ruling
key_terms.ثَوْبِي: my garment; the object affected by the saliva
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: it is nothing; an expression indicating no legal effect of impurity here

ai.seo_question: Does the saliva of a person who drinks wine make clothes najis?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on ritual purity, stating that the saliva of a person who drinks wine does not render clothing najis. The accompanying explanation clarifies that the impurity pertains to the wine itself, not to the spit of the drinker, and extends the same ruling to al-fuqqa'.
